Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Still, citizen sparrow, this vulture which you call Unnatural, let him but lumber again to air Over the rotten office, let him bear The carrion ballast up, and at the tall Tip of the sky lie cruising. Then you’ll see That no more beautiful bird is in heaven’s height, No wider more placid wings, no watchfuller flight; He shoulders nature there, the frightfully free, The naked-headed one. Pardon him, you Who dart in the orchard aisles, for it is he Devours death, mocks mutability, Has heart to make an end, keeps nature new. Thinking of Noah, childheart, try to forget How for so many bedlam hours his saw Soured the song of birds with its wheezy gnaw, And the slam of his hammer all the day beset The people’s ears. Forget that he could bear To see the towns like coral under the keel, And the fields so dismal deep. Try rather to feel How high and weary it was, on the waters where He rocked his only world, and everyone’s. Forgive the hero, you who would have died Gladly with all you knew; he rode that tide To Ararat; all men are Noah’s sons.

Even so, little sparrow of the town, consider this vulture you brand as monstrous. Just watch him heave himself back into the sky above the decaying carcass, hoisting his cargo of dead flesh, and settle into a slow glide at the very peak of heaven. In that moment you'll recognize that no bird in the sky is lovelier than he is—none has broader or calmer wings, none watches more keenly as it flies. Up there he bears the weight of the natural world upon his shoulders, that terrifyingly liberated creature with the bare head. You who flit among the rows of fruit trees should forgive him, because he is the one who feasts on death, who laughs at decay and change, who has the courage to finish things off and thereby renews the world.

When you remember Noah, innocent one, do your best to overlook how, through countless maddening hours, the rasping of his saw ruined the birds' singing with its grating scrape, and how the pounding of his hammer troubled everyone's hearing all day long. Overlook that he could stand to watch entire cities sink like coral beneath his ship's hull, and the drowned fields lying so terribly far below. Instead, attempt to understand how lofty and exhausting it was out on those waters, where he cradled the one world he possessed—which belonged to all of us too. Grant your pardon to this hero, you who would have happily perished alongside everything familiar to you. He sailed that flood all the way to Ararat, and every one of us descends from Noah.

# The Vulture and the Ark: Reflections on the Misunderstood

## The Majesty of the Vulture

We call the vulture unnatural, and we recoil from its ugliness. Yet there is a moment when all such judgments fall away—when the bird ascends to the very height of the sky. There, soaring at tremendous altitude, the vulture transforms before our eyes into something supremely beautiful and majestic. Distance and elevation reveal what our proximity had concealed: a creature of extraordinary grace, master of the highest winds.

If the vulture deserves our pardon—and it does—it is because of the sacred work it performs. It devours death itself, consuming what would otherwise fester and rot. In doing so, it mocks mutability, refusing to let decay hold dominion over the earth. Through its appetite, nature is cleansed and renewed; the vulture disposes of corruption and clears the way for life to begin again. What we called repulsive is, in truth, an agent of restoration.

## The Labor of Noah

A similar reconsideration is owed to Noah. His was not a glorious task but a tedious one. Hour after irritating hour, he bent to the labor of building his ark, and the endless work disrupted whatever peace surrounded him, silencing the ordinary songs of his days. There was nothing romantic in the sawing of timber and the fitting of planks—only weariness, and the grinding persistence that his mission demanded.

Beyond this physical toil lay a heavier burden still. Noah bore the immense weight of witnessing the entire world drowned beneath the flood. He watched creation perish while he alone was charged with preserving the only world that remained. To hold within one fragile vessel the last hope of all living things—this was a weariness of the soul that no mere carpenter could imagine.

And so, if Noah too must be forgiven for whatever faults or frailties marked him, let it be for this: he carried humanity through the flood and brought us safely to rest upon Ararat. Every person who lives descends from that voyage. He is the father of us all, and in his labor and endurance we find our common origin.
outputs.L4:
# On the Vulture and Noah: A Defense of the Maligned

This poem unfolds as two linked meditations, each taking up the cause of a figure that common judgment has cast aside. In the first, the poet turns to the vulture—that dark silhouette wheeling over the wasteland, the bird whose very name has become a byword for greed and morbid patience. In the second, the poem considers Noah, the survivor of the flood, a man whose story is too often reduced to a tale of divine wrath and grim endurance. Both stand accused: the one of feasting on death, the other of outliving a drowned world. Yet the poem argues that we have judged them wrongly, and that within their seemingly repellent or destructive roles lies a hidden service to life itself.

## The Vulture's Work

Consider first the vulture, so easily despised. We recoil from its diet, from the way it descends upon what has fallen, from the patience with which it waits beside the dying. But the poem asks us to look again. What the vulture consumes is not life but death—the carcass that would otherwise fester, the rot that would poison the land. In devouring what has ended, the vulture clears the ground for what will begin. It is not a harbinger of decay but its remedy, transforming corruption back into the clean and open air.

Through this reappraisal, the poem reveals a startling truth: the vulture "keeps nature new." Far from being an agent of death, it is death's undertaker and, in that role, life's quiet servant. Every carcass it strips away is a space returned to the living, a cycle completed so that renewal may follow. What we mistook for ugliness is in fact a necessary grace, the mechanism by which the world refreshes itself and refuses to drown in its own remains.

## Noah's Endurance

The second meditation carries this same logic into the human world. Noah, too, has been misread. We remember the flood as catastrophe, and we sometimes see in Noah only a stern figure, a survivor whose salvation came at the cost of a vanished world. But the poem reframes his endurance as an act of preservation rather than mere survival. In riding out the deluge, in keeping faith through the long dark of the storm, Noah held humanity's future intact when everything else was swept away.

His was not a passive escape but an active safeguarding. To endure the flood was to carry forward the possibility of every life that would come after—to be the thread by which the human story was not severed but continued. What looked like the world's end became, through his persistence, the world's beginning again. Noah, like the vulture, stands at the threshold between destruction and renewal, and his role is to ensure that something survives the crossing.

## The Poem's Argument

Taken together, these two meditations make a single, unified claim. The vulture and Noah are not opposites but companions in a shared truth: that survival and renewal often depend upon the very figures we are quickest to condemn. We judge by surface—by the vulture's grim feast, by Noah's lonely endurance—and in doing so we miss the deeper work being done. Life does not renew itself only through what is beautiful and gentle; it renews itself through what devours death and what outlasts catastrophe.

In defending its two maligned figures, the poem asks us to reconsider our whole habit of judgment. It suggests that the repellent and the destructive may, on closer looking, prove essential—that the world is kept new not in spite of such figures but because of them. What we scorn may be exactly what preserves us, and the future may rest, unnoticed, in hands we were too hasty to despise.
outputs.L5:
# The Frozen Moment

There was something deeply unsettling about how **still** the house had become. Where laughter once echoed through the hallways, only silence remained, thick and heavy like a blanket that refused to lift.

Sarah stood in the doorway, watching the afternoon light filter through the dusty windows. The stillness felt **unnatural**, as though the very air had forgotten how to move. Nothing stirred—not the curtains, not the leaves outside, not even the old grandfather clock that had ticked faithfully for decades.

She had spent years dreading this exact moment, and now that it was finally **over**, she wasn't sure what she felt. Relief, perhaps. Or maybe something closer to emptiness. The long chapter of caring, of waiting, of holding her breath through endless uncertain nights had come to its quiet conclusion.

Walking slowly through the rooms, she traced her fingers along the familiar surfaces. The **unnatural** quiet seemed to press against her, demanding acknowledgment. Life had a rhythm once, a natural cadence of coming and going, of routine and surprise. Now everything remained **still**, suspended in a strange kind of limbo between what was and what would be.

But endings, she reminded herself, were never truly final. When one story is **over**, another quietly begins. The stillness would eventually break. The unnatural silence would fill again with new voices, new footsteps, new life.

She opened the window and let the fresh air rush in. The curtains fluttered. Somewhere, a bird began to sing.

The world, it seemed, was ready to move forward once more.

counterfactuals.output:
You're likely thinking of **"Vulture" by Robinson Jeffers**, published in his posthumous collection *The Beginning and the End* (1963). Jeffers died in 1962, placing it squarely in the mid-20th century.

In the poem, the speaker is lying on a hillside when he notices a vulture circling above, gradually descending as it examines him as potential prey. Rather than recoiling, Jeffers finds the bird magnificent and reflects on what it would mean to be consumed by it—to be assimilated into the vulture's flesh, wings, and eyes after death. He closes with the memorable notion that such a fate would be a kind of "enskyment"—a sublime transformation and elevation—rather than something grim.

It's a characteristic Jeffers piece, reflecting his philosophy of "inhumanism," which decentered humanity and celebrated the wild, non-human natural world on its own terms. The vulture, often seen as repulsive, becomes in his hands a creature of grandeur and dignity.

# The Weight of Unsaid Things

*A Villanelle*

I never told you all the words I kept,
The tender ones I hoarded out of pride.
And now you're gone, and I am left to weep.

The clock ran fast while both of us still slept
In separate rooms where our resentments died.
I never told you all the words I kept.

Forgiveness is a debt I should have swept
Clean from the ledger where our grievance lied.
And now you're gone, and I am left to weep.

I built my walls of silence, stone by step,
And called it strength each time I turned aside.
I never told you all the words I kept.

Death does not wait for promises unwept
Or second chances carefully applied—
And now you're gone, and I am left to weep.

So let this be the vow I finally kept:
To love the living fiercely, open-eyed.
I never told you all the words I kept.
And now you're gone, and I am left to weep.

---

**About this form:** A villanelle uses nineteen lines with two repeating refrains (here, lines 1 and 3) that alternate through five tercets and reunite in the final quatrain. The obsessive return of these lines mirrors the way grief and regret circle back on themselves—fitting for exploring mortality and the ache of forgiveness that comes too late.
